memory_leads.lead: Container inland execution separates carrier haulage from merchant/shipper-arranged haulage: the ocean carrier may control or procure the inland leg in one shipment while the cargo interest controls it in another, changing who bears coordination and capacity risk.

Drayage is the short-haul connector between marine terminal, rail ramp, depot, warehouse/CFS or customer; even short distances can become a critical constraint because they require synchronized container, chassis/truck, driver, appointment and receiving readiness.

Marine-terminal gate handoff is a custody and eligibility state: cargo/container availability, release status, appointment or queue, documentation and equipment readiness must align before a box can physically leave or enter the terminal.

Rail intermodal ramps create a second terminal system inland, with train capacity, cutoff, loading/unloading, container grounding and pickup states; port discharge does not imply immediate inland availability.

On-dock versus off-dock rail changes the number and type of handoffs between vessel terminal and rail network; an additional truck transfer can add flexibility but also extra queue, custody and synchronization risk.

Inland barge or short-sea feeder-like container moves can substitute for road or rail on suitable corridors, creating another scheduled capacity layer with terminal and connection dependencies rather than a generic trucking alternative.

Inland container depots and dry ports can move storage, empty handling, customs-related processing or intermodal transfer away from the marine terminal, effectively extending parts of the port interface inland without eliminating handoff risk.

Container freight stations support stuffing/stripping, consolidation and deconsolidation, especially for less-than-container-load cargo; the box movement and the underlying cargo movement can therefore have different custody and timing states.

Warehouses and distribution centers are active nodes in container-cycle time: receiving capacity, unloading labor/equipment, yard space and appointment availability can keep an import box occupied or delay export cargo readiness after the ocean leg is operationally complete.

Gate and delivery appointment systems ration scarce handling windows across terminals, depots and warehouses; appointment scarcity can convert nominal truck/container availability into unusable capacity.

Inland cutoffs and connection windows matter like marine cutoffs: missing a rail train, barge departure, terminal receiving window or vessel cutoff can add a discrete cycle of delay rather than a smooth incremental transit penalty.

Empty return, reuse or triangulation/street-turn style moves can shorten equipment cycles by matching an import empty directly to a nearby export need instead of routing it through a depot, but require compatible commercial and operational states.

Cargo release and availability states may depend on several parties and events—carrier/document release, terminal availability, customs or inspection status, inland booking and receiving readiness—so physical proximity to the consignee does not equal deliverability.

Effective container capacity is end-to-end and bottlenecked by the minimum usable state across ocean slot, box/chassis, terminal gate, inland mode and receiving node; adding capacity at one stage may not increase delivered throughput.

P019 schedule unreliability can propagate nonlinearly inland: vessel bunching sends concentrated container volumes into gates, rail ramps, warehouses and trucking fleets, creating congestion even if average weekly inland capacity appears adequate.
P017 equipment-cycle time should include customer/warehouse dwell, inland repositioning and return-to-depot or terminal states, not stop when a container crosses the marine-terminal gate.

Point-in-time replay should distinguish physical movement events from availability/release/appointment events because a container can be at an inland node before the commercial or operational system exposes it as actionable.
The general claim that ports and inland links can become the binding shipping constraint is already explicit in the atlas; P020 only decomposes the post-terminal handoff chain.
Chassis scarcity and empty-equipment repositioning are already established in P017; P020 retains only their interactions with drayage, ramps, appointments and inland custody.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Blind recall is too regional and salience-biased for provider-level lineage or ranking.
Specific inland corridor performance, rates, train/barge schedules and capacity figures require dated Evidence.
Local gate, labor, customs, appointment and access rules vary materially by port/country and period and require Evidence.
Commercial responsibility and legal/tariff effects require claim-scoped Evidence rather than blind recall.

stop_reason: The post-terminal inland chain is populated from haulage choice and drayage through gate/ramp, rail/barge, ICD/CFS/warehouse and connection/return states; further recall becomes provider-, corridor-, country-, tariff-, labor-rule- or procedure-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no provider, corridor rate/capacity, haulage term, gate/customs/labor rule, transit time, schedule or historical inland event is verified.
